1170.title: Vaisheshika (atoms)
1170.hook: tip a candle and the flame still climbs upward, and the Vaisheshika Sutra names the unseen thing behind it
1170.howItsDone: In the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition, adrishta is taught as the unseen result of past actions, and later thinkers such as Udayana argued that Ishvara guides it; students meet these arguments after learning the categories.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika's list of substances ended with the self, known by the breath, and the mind, a gate for one thing at a time. Today, its last day.
screen: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.` · `VAISHESHIKA, A LAST DAY.`

segments.voice: Light a candle and tilt it. The wax leans, the wick leans, and the flame doesn't. It keeps climbing straight up, as if something above were calling. Step outside, and the wind isn't climbing. It runs sideways across the field. Nobody taught the flame to rise or the wind to run. A school that explains the world with atoms and categories has to say something about that: why does anything start moving the way it does? The Vaisheshika Sutra answers in a single line, with a word that means, simply, unseen.
screen: `TILT THE CANDLE.` → `THE FLAME STILL CLIMBS.` → `WHY DOES ANYTHING MOVE?`

segments.voice: The word is adrishta: the unseen. The Sutra says fire's flaming upward, wind's blowing sideways, the first movement of the atoms and the first movement of the mind are all caused by adrishta. So what is it? In this school, the unseen force is bound up with what beings have done. Actions leave something behind, merit and its opposite, and that unseen residue helps shape what happens next, down to how atoms first come together into a world fit for those who will live in it. Atoms, categories, and underneath them, the moral weight of what we do: the dharma the Sutra opened with, showing up again at the bottom of physics. Then there's God. Near its opening, the Sutra says the Veda is authoritative because it is the word of That. Commentators read That in different ways. Some read it as God, Ishvara. Others read it as dharma, which the Veda teaches. Later thinkers in the joined Nyaya-Vaisheshika school, Udayana among them, argued at length that the unseen needs a knower to guide it, and that the knower is Ishvara, who sets the atoms moving in keeping with what beings have earned. So within one school, some readers see God in that line and some see dharma. Vaisheshika leaves you with this. The world is made of tiny, lasting things, sorted into kinds, each one particular. And moving through all of it is something you'll never see directly: the weight of what's been done.
screen: `ADRISHTA: THE UNSEEN.` · `FIRE RISES, WIND RUNS SIDEWAYS.` · `WHAT WE DO LEAVES SOMETHING BEHIND.` · `THAT: GOD, OR DHARMA?` · then, large: `THE WEIGHT OF WHAT'S BEEN DONE.`

segments.voice: Light a candle and watch the flame rise, or picture one, or simply watch your breath rise and fall. Then think of one small thing you did yesterday, a kind word, a sharp one, a promise kept or dropped, and without judging it, notice that what it left behind is still somewhere, moving things a little. If you pray, you can hold yesterday's actions before Ishvara, or the name of God you use.
Vaisheshika. The school of atoms, categories and particulars, where even the first motion of the world runs on adrishta, the unseen left behind by what we do.
Your line: Vaisheshika, atoms. Even a deed that nobody sees still leaves something behind. Until tomorrow.

1171.title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
1171.hook: the Samkhya Karika begins the way a doctor does: there is pain, and the remedies on hand don't finish the job
1171.howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and it is taught alongside Yoga, its paired school among the darshanas.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vaisheshika closed with adrishta, the unseen left behind by what we do. A third school opens today.

A headache, again. You take something for it, and it works, for a while. Then it's back next week. A bad night of worry: you call a friend, it helps, and two nights later it's back. A storm takes out the power and there's nothing to do but wait. Some pain comes from inside us, some from other people, some from the weather and the world. The fixes in the drawer are real, but they don't finish the job. Today's school opens right there, the way a good doctor would, by asking what actually ends it.
screen: `THE HEADACHE COMES BACK.` → `THE FIXES IN THE DRAWER.` → `WHAT ACTUALLY ENDS IT?`

segments.voice: The school is Samkhya. Tradition names the sage Kapila as its source, and it's usually read through a short book of verses, the Samkhya Karika. Its first verse says: because we are struck by three kinds of pain, we want to know what removes it. Commentators sort them as the hook did: pain from within, in body and mind; pain from other beings; and pain from forces beyond us. Then an objector speaks. Why bother with philosophy? There's medicine. It doesn't say medicine is bad. It says the seen remedies are not certain and not final. The pain returns. The second verse goes further: even the rituals of the Veda are like the seen remedies. They help, but they come with flaws and they wear off. Better, the verse says, is knowing three things: what is manifest, what is unmanifest, and the knower. That's where the counting comes in. Some take the name Samkhya to mean counting, others discernment; either way, the school goes through reality item by item. Its third verse sorts everything into a root that comes from nothing else, things that come from it and give rise to more, and things that only come from others. Add them up and you have twenty-four principles. And one more stands outside the count, neither made nor making anything. It comes tomorrow. Samkhya doesn't start with God or with atoms. It starts with pain, and an honest question about what really ends it.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PAIN.` · `SEEN REMEDIES DON'T FINISH IT.` · `KNOW THE WORLD, AND THE KNOWER.` · `TWENTY-FOUR, AND ONE MORE.` · then, large: `IT STARTS WITH PAIN.`

segments.voice: Count ten breaths, starting again at one if you lose count. Then bring to mind one pain you're carrying and simply sort it, from within, from another person, or from the world, noticing that something in you can name it. If you pray, you can hold that pain before God. If it's ever too heavy, or you think of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.
Samkhya. A school that begins with three kinds of pain, looks for what truly ends it, and counts out the world, twenty-four principles and one more.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. The fixes in the drawer help, but don't finish the job. Same time tomorrow.

1172.title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
1172.hook: a film plays in a dark room, and someone is watching it: Samkhya's first two
1172.howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and its map of purusha and prakriti is taught alongside the Yoga Sutras, which build on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday Samkhya opened with pain and a count: twenty-four principles, plus one standing outside it.

A film is playing on a laptop in a dark room. A storm, a car chase, a wedding, a funeral. The light on the wall keeps changing color. On the couch, somebody is watching. The storm doesn't get them wet. The funeral doesn't bury them. And yet without them, nobody would be seeing any of it. So there are two things in that room: everything that shows up on the screen, and the one it shows up for. Samkhya starts its whole count right there, with two that never blend. Today, their names.
screen: `A FILM IN A DARK ROOM.` → `SOMEONE IS WATCHING.` → `TWO THAT NEVER BLEND.`

segments.voice: The first is prakriti. The Samkhya Karika, the book of verses from yesterday, calls it the root, and says the root is not itself made by anything. Everything else unfolds out of it. Mountains and rivers, yes. Your body, yes. But here's the surprise: your senses, your mind, your thoughts and even your sense of being an I all sit on prakriti's side of the line. In Samkhya, thinking is part of nature. A worry is as much a thing in the world as a cloud. The second is purusha. The Karika describes it in a short string of words: a witness, a seer, neutral, standing apart, not the one doing anything. Purusha doesn't think the thoughts. It's the one they appear in front of. And the Karika says there isn't just one purusha. It reasons this way: people are born separately, die separately, and have their own senses, so each has a purusha of their own. Other schools see this point differently. Advaita Vedanta, one of the Vedanta schools still to come, reads the self as one. Samkhya keeps many, and the schools are allowed to disagree. So what does this change in a day? It moves a line most of us draw without looking. A wave of irritation, a plan for dinner, a memory from school: Samkhya would put all of them on the screen. Something in you is watching the film. Samkhya's name for that something is purusha.
screen: `PRAKRITI: THE ROOT, NOT MADE.` · `THOUGHTS SIT ON NATURE'S SIDE.` · `PURUSHA: THE WITNESS.` · `MANY WITNESSES, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Let things show up for a couple of minutes, a sound from the street, an itch, a thought about tomorrow, and each time, neither push it away nor follow it; just note, quietly, seen. Sounds, feelings and thoughts all go on the same screen. If you pray, you can let a prayer be one more thing that shows up, and is seen.
Samkhya. A school of thought that counts out the world, and starts with two: purusha, the one who sees, and prakriti, everything seen.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. A worry is on the screen, not in the one watching. Rest well.

1173.title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
1173.hook: same desk, same book, three different mornings: Samkhya's three gunas
1173.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use the three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, as a way of speaking about food, moods and habits, and the Bhagavad Gita also teaches the three gunas.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: purusha, the witness, and prakriti, everything it sees, thoughts included.

Three mornings, one desk, one book, one student. On the first morning, every page lands. The ideas are clear, the room is quiet, the hour flies. On the second morning, she can't stay put. She checks her phone, gets water, reorganizes the pens, plans the whole semester. On the third morning, she reads one paragraph four times and none of it goes in. Same desk. Same book. Same person. Something underneath changed. Samkhya has a name for that something, and it says the whole world is woven out of it.
screen: `SAME DESK, SAME BOOK.` → `CLEAR, RESTLESS, HEAVY.` → `WHAT CHANGED?`

segments.voice: Today Samkhya opens up prakriti, the root. It is made of three gunas, a word often translated as strands or qualities. The Samkhya Karika describes them in a single verse. Sattva is light and it shows things: it's the clear morning. Rajas stirs and moves: it's the restless one. Tamas is heavy and it covers: it's the paragraph read four times. Everything on prakriti's side, a stone, a meal, a mood, a thought, is some mix of the three. Here's what's easy to get wrong. The gunas aren't heroes and villains. The Karika says they work together, each one leaning on the others and taking its turn on top. Without rajas nothing gets started. Without tamas nothing holds still long enough to sleep. And the Karika gives them a picture: they work for one purpose, the way a lamp does. Commentators spell it out. A lamp needs oil, a wick and a flame, three different things, and together they make one light. A few days ago, Vaisheshika took the world apart into tiny pieces, atoms. Samkhya takes it apart a different way, into strands that are woven through everything at once. Two schools, two lenses, and neither one is asked to beat the other. So when a morning is heavy or racing, Samkhya doesn't call it a failure. It calls it a mix, and mixes shift.
screen: `PRAKRITI HAS THREE STRANDS.` · `LIGHT, MOTION, WEIGHT.` · `NOT HEROES AND VILLAINS.` · `ONE LAMP: OIL, WICK, FLAME.`

segments.voice: Check in with what's here right now: something restless, an urge to move or plan; something heavy, a pull toward sleep or a fog; something clear. There's no right answer and no score; just notice the mix, and notice that it shifts, even inside two minutes. If you pray, you can offer whatever mix you find, just as it is.
Samkhya. The school that sees prakriti woven from three gunas: sattva, light and clear; rajas, moving; tamas, heavy. Together, like a lamp, they make one light.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. The strands take turns on top. See you tomorrow.

1174.title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
1174.hook: a ringtone in a crowded airport, and a dozen hands reach for a dozen pockets: buddhi and ahamkara
1174.howItsDone: Students of Samkhya, and of the Yoga traditions that use its map, learn the unfolding of prakriti in order, from buddhi and ahamkara down to the elements, and some teachers use it as a contemplation.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: the three gunas, light, motion and weight, working together like oil, wick and flame.

A phone rings at a crowded gate in an airport. It's the default ringtone, the one nobody bothers to change. And a dozen hands go to a dozen pockets at once. Mine? Mine? Nobody decided to reach. The reach came first, and the checking came after. There's a little engine in people that keeps tagging things as mine: my phone, my seat, my idea, my turn. Samkhya noticed that engine. It gave it a name, and it put it in a surprising place in the order of the world. Today, the unfolding from the root, two steps out.
screen: `ONE RINGTONE, A DOZEN HANDS.` → `MINE? MINE?` → `THE ENGINE THAT SAYS MINE.`

segments.voice: The Samkhya Karika lays out the order. From prakriti, the root, comes the great one, mahat, which the text also calls buddhi. From buddhi comes ahamkara. And from ahamkara comes everything after it, the senses, the mind and the stuff of the elements. Take them one at a time. Buddhi, the Karika says, is marked by deciding. It's the part that settles a question: this, not that. Ahamkara, the next step, is marked by the claim of I. Translators often render it as ego, or the I-maker. It's the engine in the airport, the reach that says mine before anyone checks. Now notice the order, because it's the strange part. In Samkhya, deciding and the sense of me come before earth and water. The world doesn't build up from dust into a mind at the end. It unfolds from the inside out, intelligence first, then the I, then the senses and the elements. And notice the side of the line. Buddhi and ahamkara both belong to prakriti. They're instruments, finely made, but they're not purusha, the witness from two days ago. That's the turn Samkhya asks for. The voice in the head that says my turn, my seat, my idea, isn't the seer. It's one more thing being seen. Some Hindu schools read the self and the ego very differently, and they'll have their say in the weeks ahead. Samkhya's map is simple and bold: the I-maker is a tool, and tools can be noticed.
screen: `ROOT, THEN BUDDHI, THEN AHAMKARA.` · `BUDDHI DECIDES.` · `AHAMKARA SAYS I.` · `BOTH ARE TOOLS, NOT THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Let your mind wander where it likes, and each time a thought carries a tag, my plans, my problem, my body, my people, just notice the tag. You don't have to remove it, since things really are yours to care for; only notice how quickly the tag arrives, and that something is watching it arrive. If you pray, you can hand one of those tagged things over, quietly, in your own way.
Samkhya. Its map unfolds from the root: first buddhi, which decides, then ahamkara, which says I. Both on nature's side of the line.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. Mine is a reflex that arrives before anyone checks. I'll be here tomorrow.

1175.title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
1175.hook: packing up a kitchen box by box, and Samkhya's inventory of everything
1175.howItsDone: Some students of Samkhya memorize the list of principles, the tattvas, from prakriti down to the elements, and teachers in Samkhya and Yoga lineages use it as a map for contemplation.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Samkhya: buddhi, which decides, and ahamkara, the I-maker that says mine.

Moving day. The kitchen has to go into boxes, and the only way through it is a list. Plates. Glasses. The pans, which nest. The drawer of things nobody can name. Halfway through, something happens. Listing it all makes the kitchen strange. You see objects you've walked past for years. A list isn't just a record. It's a way of looking. Samkhya made an inventory too, and a much bigger one: everything that exists, sorted into a short list of principles. A few days ago came the outline of that count. Today the boxes open, and everything inside gets a name.
screen: `MOVING DAY.` → `A LIST IS A WAY OF LOOKING.` → `OPENING THE BOXES.`

segments.voice: The Samkhya Karika sorts everything with one question: does it come from something, and does something come from it? The root, prakriti, makes but isn't made. Then the Karika names seven that are both made and making: the great one, buddhi; the I-maker, ahamkara; and five subtle elements, the bare potentials of sound, touch, form, taste and smell. Then it names sixteen that are made and make nothing further. Ten of them are the organs. Five take in the world: ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose. Five act on it: speech, hands, feet, and the organs of release and of birth. One more is manas, the mind, which the Karika says shares in both kinds, turning what comes in into a plan. And the last five are the elements you can stub your toe on: space, air, fire, water, earth. One root, seven, sixteen. Now the twenty-four principles in the title have names. And then the Karika names one more thing, and it's set apart from the whole list: purusha, which is neither made nor making. Look at what the inventory does. Everything on the list but the root comes from something, and all of it changes. Your senses, your mind, your sense of I, the floor under you. Purusha is the one thing that doesn't come out of a box. Some students of Samkhya learn this list by heart, not as trivia, but so that, looking at anything, they can ask where it sits in the count.
screen: `ONE QUESTION: MADE, OR MAKING?` · `THE ROOT, THEN SEVEN, THEN SIXTEEN.` · `SENSES, MIND, ELEMENTS.` · `PURUSHA STANDS OUTSIDE THE COUNT.`

segments.voice: Go slowly through the list in your own body: hearing, touch where your weight lands, seeing even with eyes closed, tasting, smelling; then your hands, your feet, your voice at rest, and the mind, already making plans. Each one is on the list. Then rest, and let the one who's been noticing all of it stay unnamed.
Samkhya. Its inventory: one root, seven made and making, sixteen made only. Twenty-four principles, and purusha, the witness, outside the list.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. Everything on the list changes; the witness isn't on it. Go gently.

1176.title: the Samkhya Karika)
1176.hook: a bed doesn't sleep in itself: how the Samkhya Karika argues for a witness it can't point to
1176.howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is read verse by verse with classical commentaries such as Gaudapada's, and its arguments, like the one for purusha, are studied alongside the replies of other schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, everything in Samkhya's count got a name: senses, mind, elements and the rest, with purusha outside the list.
screen: `THE WHOLE COUNT, NAMED.` · `A BED FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: A bed doesn't sleep in itself. Somebody built a frame, stretched the slats, laid the mattress, smoothed the sheet, folded the blanket at the foot. Every part was fitted to every other part. And the whole thing is plainly for someone who isn't part of the bed. Nobody looks at a made bed and thinks it was arranged for the benefit of the pillow. That's an ordinary thought, and the Samkhya Karika builds an argument on it. From today, the Karika itself, starting with its question: how can anyone know the witness is there at all?
screen: `A BED DOESN'T SLEEP IN ITSELF.` → `ARRANGED FOR SOMEONE.` → `HOW DO WE KNOW THE WITNESS?`

segments.voice: First, the book. Near its end, the Samkhya Karika tells its own family tree. The teaching came from the sage Kapila, who passed it to Asuri, who passed it to Panchashikha, and through a line of students it reached Ishvarakrishna, who set it down in these verses. Now the problem. Purusha never acts. It doesn't think, decide or move. So how could anyone know it's there? The Karika answers in one verse with a short string of reasons, and the first is the bed. Whatever is put together, it says, exists for the sake of another. Commentators make it concrete with exactly that picture: a bed, made of parts, for a sleeper who isn't one of the parts. Now look at a body. Bones, breath, senses, a mind, a sense of I, all fitted together. Samkhya asks: for whom? Not for the parts. For someone outside the assembly. The verse adds more. There has to be something beyond the three gunas. There has to be one the whole thing is overseen for, and one who experiences it. And people strive for release, which makes no sense unless someone is there to be released. Notice what kind of argument this is. Samkhya can't point at purusha. It infers it, the way you'd infer a sleeper from a carefully made bed. You may find the argument convincing or not; other schools weigh it differently. But it's an honest move: reasoning from ordinary things to what can't be seen.
screen: `KAPILA TO ISHVARAKRISHNA.` · `PURUSHA NEVER ACTS. HOW DO WE KNOW?` · `WHAT'S PUT TOGETHER IS FOR ANOTHER.` · `INFERRED, NOT POINTED AT.`

segments.voice: Notice the arrangement you are right now: the spine holding you up, the lungs filling, the heart keeping time, the ears taking in the room. Let the whole assembly be felt at once, then rest in the simple fact that it's all being experienced, and leave the one experiencing it unnamed. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own words for the body that's been made.
The Samkhya Karika. Ishvarakrishna's verses on Samkhya, which reason that whatever is put together, like a bed, is for someone outside it: purusha.
